title: A contract crosses a boundary
text:
Start with one state transition 
 A Compact contract is more than the text of a circuit. Its behavior includes the value returned, the ledger reads and writes, the witnesses called, the cost charged, the statement proved, and the transaction that eventually changes state. A second backend has to preserve those relationships. 
 Imagine a counter that increments and returns its new value. A generated Rust function can calculate the right number while recording the wrong ledger operation. A recorder can produce the right operations while preparing a proof for a different installed verifier. A valid proof can still fail a funded ledger application. Each of those failures occupies a different boundary. 
 Our journey began with a TypeScript-oriented Compact compiler and a Ledger 8 reference environment. The long-term question was whether Rust could become an ergonomic, typed way to use the same contract semantics. The answer emerged through repeated small deliveries rather than one replacement compiler. 
 What this book preserves 
 This edition follows the original Rust text emitter, the Rust AST rebuild, native execution, recorded execution, proof and wallet integration, the 0.3.0 closure, compositional effects, the functional Ledger 8 experiment, and the move to Ledger 9. 
 Every chapter asks four questions. What limitation triggered the work? Which owner changed? What behavior became possible? Which evidence established the result? A final section records what was still open at that point. 
 The commit explorer is the granular index. Phase assignments are editorial groupings over a frozen Git graph. Commit subjects are historical source material. They sometimes use shorthand or describe an intended result. The chapter narrative and its receipts supply the scope of acceptance. 
 Three ways to read 
 Read the chapters in order for the engineering story. Follow the Architecture link to walk a circuit through the pipeline. Use the Commit explorer to move from a milestone to its individual steps, then follow a published commit back to code. 
 The historical atlas preserves the earlier October documentation as an explicitly dated snapshot. The later chapters explain which earlier limitations were subsequently resolved. 
 The edition boundary 
 The mainstream compatibility reference is LFDT-Minokawa/compact at 672bd0f226f47a7d036c5c074ce71fbe1af1925e. Released Compact 0.36.0 and the Ledger 9.1.0.1 SDK package matrix supply a separate interoperability reference. The local compatibility checkpoint used for this edition is v73 on November 13, 2026. 
 PR #725 merged the migration foundation into the working branch. The broad upstream-compatibility work continued locally afterward. Two final isolated commits in this edition await canonical integration. A merged foundation and complete upstream compatibility are distinct milestones. 
 Why the distinctions matter 
 A guide becomes misleading when a reader cannot tell whether an example was merely generated, executed natively, proved, or applied to a ledger. This book keeps those stages visible. It also keeps historical Ledger 8 evidence useful while explaining the changed Ledger 9 SDK and representation contracts. 
 The objective remains faithful Compact behavior with useful Rust types, explicit diagnostics, and runtime checks where values cross an untrusted boundary.

title: TypeScript and fixed ground
text:
Why begin with the existing backend 
 The TypeScript path already connected Compact source to the ledger runtime and proof ecosystem. It provided generated contract interfaces, native host execution, witness callbacks, ledger operations, and the data used to construct proof statements. Reusing its behavior as a reference gave the Rust work something more precise than an aesthetic target. 
 Ledger 8 provided a stable package family. The compiler, on-chain VM, serialization, field arithmetic, cryptography and proof tooling could be pinned together. When a Rust state differed from a TypeScript state, the team could investigate the representation or operation instead of first reconciling two changing protocol generations. 
 The ledger stays authoritative 
 The Rust runtime reused the ledger's field, FAB alignment, state, VM, serialization and proof primitives. FAB is the aligned representation used to move values across these boundaries. A contract-level type can occupy several aligned atoms. Equal-looking host values do not establish identical serialized statements. 
 The counter example makes this concrete. A read should use the ledger operation and cost model for that slot. Replacing it with an independent Rust calculation could return the same number while missing the protocol's behavior. 
 What TypeScript captures taught us 
 Independent captures became a recurring technique. Generate a reference contract with a known compiler/runtime pair, execute selected calls, and retain the inputs, full state bytes, transcript, gas and expected refusal. Generated Rust then consumes the same scenario. 
 These captures are stronger than comparing a few printed values. They can detect a wrong state tag, an incorrect atom width, a reordered witness, a changed private transcript or a different gas path. They also need their own provenance. A capture generated by a mismatched runtime is an unreliable reference. 
 An important lineage correction 
 The selected Rust AST line is based on the Ledger 8 revision eb72a5ab6085bf9b8564cc80c98c973e04825c2d. The retained original Rust oracle is another Ledger 8 line. Git does not place oracle revision 589c92ef below that exact eb72a5ab commit. Their shared ancestor is earlier. 
 The architectural comparison is still meaningful. The diagram should show two Ledger 8 lines sharing a wider history, with the original used as a behavior oracle for the AST rebuild. It should avoid inventing a direct parent relationship. 
 What was solved 
 A pinned reference made differential tests interpretable. The project could change the Rust architecture while retaining a stable account of source behavior and ledger representation. 
 What was still open 
 Reference captures cover named cases. They cannot establish whole-language equivalence by themselves. That gap later motivated capability inventories, source refusals, broader fixture matrices and proof/application gates.

title: TypeScript and Rust AST
text:
Why add a Rust AST backend? 
 The Rust AST backend lets a Rust application call generated Compact code through types that preserve more of the contract’s meaning. A bounded integer carries its limit. A fixed Vector carries its element type and length. A circuit call consumes a context and returns the next one. These choices make several host-side mistakes visible while compiling the application. 
 The compiler also gains a structured way to build Rust. It checks a typed internal program, lowers admitted operations and constructs Rust syntax trees. That gives contributors explicit places to implement a language feature and diagnose unsupported cases. 
 The TypeScript backend supplies generated contract interfaces, witness callbacks, ledger access and proof data for JavaScript applications. It has typed declarations and runtime checks of its own. The comparison below follows the implementations and tests retained in the November 13, 2026 book edition. 
 How the two paths work 
 
 
 TypeScript backend 
  Compact source
  → shared frontend checks
  → TypeScript-oriented lowering
  → JavaScript + TypeScript declarations
  → Compact TypeScript runtime
  → ledger operations and proof inputs
  
 The application imports a generated Contract class and calls a method such as  contract.circuits.increment_by(context, 7n) . The result contains the successor context, return value, gas and proof data. 
 This path fits applications already using Node.js, TypeScript and the existing JavaScript SDK integration. 
 
 
 Rust AST backend 
  Compact source
  → shared frontend checks
  → versioned typed IR
  → checked semantic lowering
  → structured Rust syntax
  → generated crate + typed runtime
  → ledger operations and proof inputs
  
 The application imports generated Rust functions or contract wrappers. A call such as  increment_by(context, amount)  returns a  Result  containing the execution result and successor context. 
 This path fits Rust services and tools that need generated Compact APIs in the same language as their application. 
 
 
 Both paths begin with Compact’s frontend checks. Source typing and disclosure rules apply before host code is emitted. Rust’s generated interface adds checks at the application boundary, where developers supply arguments and connect calls. 
  Read the checked Rust pipeline  ·  Read the TypeScript reference workflow  
 Benefits for application developers 
 Keep contract meaning in the argument types 
 Consider the same Counter contract used in the walkthrough. Its amount parameter is Compact  Uint<16> , which admits values from 0 through 65,535. 
 
 
 
 Surface 
 Generated argument 
 What the caller must supply 
 
 
 
 
 TypeScript 
  bigint  
 A  bigint . The generated runtime checks the value’s range. 
 
 
 Rust AST 
  BoundedUint<65535>  
 A value constructed through the bounded carrier’s checked API. The function signature preserves that bound. 
 
 
 
  let amount = BoundedUint::<65_535>::new(7)?;
let increment = increment_by(context, amount)?;
  
 The Rust compiler refuses a plain  u16  in this position. It also distinguishes carriers with different declared bounds. The integer’s value is checked when the bounded value is constructed. For example,  new(65_536)  returns an error. 
 TypeScript already rejects a  number  where the declaration expects  bigint . Rust makes the contract’s bound part of the parameter type as well. 
 Make the state handoff explicit 
 A sequence of calls needs to continue from the returned context. The Rust call takes the context by value, so the compiler tracks which binding has been consumed. 
  let increment = increment_by(context, amount)?;
let reset = reset_round(increment.context)?;
  
 Trying  reset_round(context)  after the increment produces  E0382 , “use of moved value.” In the TypeScript interface, the original and returned contexts have the same type and the caller selects which one to pass. Rust’s ownership rule catches reuse of that consumed binding before the application runs. 
  Open the complete Counter example and the locally exercised diagnostics  
 Preserve values with useful Rust types 
 
 
 
 Compact concept 
 Rust interface benefit 
 
 
 
 
  Field  
 A field carrier gives field arithmetic and representation a named owner. 
 
 
 Uint with a bounded range 
  BoundedUint  carries the admitted maximum in its type and checks construction. 
 
 
 Vector with a fixed length 
  FixedVector  carries the element type and length. Consumers can use ordinary Rust type checking for both. 
 
 
 Ledger declaration 
 A generated typed slot connects a declaration to its ledger path and read/write operations. 
 
 
 Fallible circuit or witness work 
  Result  and the  ?  operator make error propagation explicit in the generated call path. 
 
 
 
 TypeScript declarations can also express fixed tuples, products and typed method names. The Rust benefit is the combination of domain carriers, Rust ownership and ordinary compiler checking throughout a Rust consumer. 
 The Ledger 9 cryptography work extends the same approach to distinct base/scalar and point carriers. Runtime decoding validates external representations before they enter typed operations. 
  Read the generated types and typed slots  ·  Read the cryptographic carriers  
 Integrate with a Rust application directly 
 The backend emits a Cargo crate, matching runtime material and generated entry points. A Rust service can call the contract, inspect typed state and handle errors through its existing Rust code. 
 Native execution and recorded execution expose the outputs needed for different steps in the application. Recording retains the ordered public operations for replay and proof preparation. The Counter walkthrough shows the smallest local call, and the recording chapter follows the later transition to an installed operation. 
  Read recorded execution and application handoff  
 Benefits for compiler contributors 
 Build syntax as a tree 
 The Rust renderer constructs expressions, statements, blocks, paths and types using Rust syntax-tree libraries. The formatter renders those structures into readable source. 
 For example, a multiplication whose left operand is an addition is represented as a nested expression. Parentheses follow from that structure. A contributor can inspect the checked operation and the syntax node that represents it. 
  See the nested calculation before and after  
 Give each semantic decision an owner 
 A feature crosses the source frontend, typed IR, validator, lowerer, renderer and runtime. Explicit boundaries make the responsibilities reviewable. Unsupported input can produce a diagnostic while its source and operation are still identifiable. 
 The checked operation model also supports composition. A read, assertion or write can appear inside a branch or sequence. A shared semantic fold handles admitted behavior through native and recorded adapters, reducing duplicated decisions about ordering and results. 
  Explore the shapes and operations domain models  
 Test ordinary use and misuse 
 Generated-crate tests exercise the same entry points an application imports. Compile-fail cases check wrong element types, wrong Vector lengths and consumed contexts. Behavioral comparisons check return values, ledger state, witness order and gas against an independent reference. Applicable proof lanes then check the statement, verifier, funded application and replay. 
 These checks address different failure modes. A type-correct Rust expression can still select the wrong ledger slot or operand, so semantic and proof tests remain part of delivery. 
  Follow the verification stages  
 What the benefits mean for this migration 
 Rust AST is useful when the application is written in Rust and benefits from domain types, ownership, native library integration and explicit errors. TypeScript remains a direct fit for JavaScript applications and their SDK workflows. 
 Ledger 9 is a protocol migration that changes package families, ABI, serialization and transaction behavior. The typed Rust interface existed on Ledger 8 too. The Counter comparison uses Ledger 8 TypeScript and Ledger 9 Rust to show the journey while retaining each runtime’s own protocol pairing. 
 The current edition records a merged Ledger 9 foundation and selected local arm64 compatibility results. Full-corpus qualification, native Linux results for later local ports and generated joint two-contract execution have the open scopes described in their chapters. The benefits described here come from the generated APIs, compiler architecture and exercised controls. Performance depends on the workload and requires its own measurements. 
  Read the Ledger 9 migration  ·  Read the current compatibility boundary

title: The first Rust emitter
text:
The first useful proof of direction 
 The retained original Rust backend showed that Compact could produce useful Rust. Its Scheme passes operated on TypeScript-oriented compiler representations and assembled Rust source text. The original oracle's ancestry introduces the eight-file Ltypescript emitter in June 2026. 
 This was a practical implementation strategy. A compiler can reuse an already lowered representation and get a working target quickly. Generated crates and examples then make the missing operations visible. 
 Where text emission becomes expensive 
 Consider a nested expression containing a ledger read, a fallible conversion and a function call. A textual emitter must preserve the source type, track the updated context, arrange error propagation, and output legal Rust syntax. If those decisions share one string-building layer, a local feature can affect many unrelated cases. 
 A missing clone may become an ownership error. An extra conversion can change a value's admitted range. Parentheses can make syntactically legal code with the wrong grouping. Testing generated text catches some problems after emission, but the compiler still lacks a single closed place to decide whether a construct is valid for the target. 
 Why retain the original 
 The old backend supplied a valuable reference for the replacement. It contained behavior and generated-crate conventions that the new architecture had to preserve deliberately. Removing it would have discarded a comparative baseline precisely when the rebuild most needed one. 
 The project therefore used the original implementation as an oracle. The replacement could adopt a different internal design while comparing the external behavior of selected contracts. 
 The decision 
 Keep Scheme as the shared Compact frontend. Move target-specific semantic admission into a versioned internal model. Let a Rust backend construct Rust syntax through Rust syntax-tree libraries. 
 This change was about ownership of decisions. It did not require a new Compact language, a replacement ledger VM, or a parallel cryptographic specification. 
 Before and after · Emitting a nested calculation 
   
  Mermaid source  
 Before · Splice rendered expressions into text 
 An emitter for multiply-after-add must put parentheses around the rendered addition. Dropping them can produce valid Rust with different arithmetic. 
  Illustrative text emission
"(" + emit(a) + " + " + emit(b) + ") * " + emit(c)
  
 After · Represent the grouping in the tree 
 The outer multiplication receives a checked addition as its left operand. The renderer receives that structure and can emit the required parentheses. The syntax node names below are schematic. 
  Multiply(Add(a, b), c)
  
 With 2, 3 and 4, the intended result is 20. A string that comes out as 2 + 3 * 4 would give 14. This illustrates why the project tests source behavior in addition to compiling the emitted Rust. 
 A contributor's test 
 When investigating an old generated example, identify the source revision, backend line and runtime family first. Two files both called generated Rust can belong to different architectures and ABI generations. A bug fixed in the oracle is a clue for the AST line, with a separate port and test still required.

title: A closed Rust boundary
text:
The new pipeline 
 After shared Compact analysis, Chez Scheme lowered supported constructs into a versioned JSON model. Rust deserialized and checked that model, selected typed runtime operations, and built output through syn, quote, proc-macro2 and prettyplease. 
 The crucial word is supported. A closed internal representation gives each admitted node an explicit meaning. Unsupported constructs should produce a diagnostic at a known boundary. Silently manufacturing a placeholder would conceal a missing semantic case. 
 A vertical slice before a framework 
 The first slice used schema 1 for pure Field, Boolean, Unit, tuple and vector circuits, including Field addition. It explicitly refused ledger and witness constructs. Ledger-backed primitive types, Cell and Counter state changes, typed values and typed reads followed. Set, Map and List operations expanded that native surface. Pure conditionals, local bindings and circuit calls expanded the usable source subset. 
 Each slice joined several owners. Scheme supplied the source node and type. The Rust model represented it. Checked lowering established a legal operation. Syntax emission built the Rust expression. The runtime delegated ledger behavior to the VM. Generated consumers exercised the ordinary API. 
 Why structured syntax helped 
 A Rust syntax tree gives the emitter a representation for expressions, statements, blocks, paths and types. The formatter can render those nodes without encoding semantics in whitespace or string fragments. 
 That benefit has a boundary. Constructing an AST does not prove that the correct field operation or source conversion was chosen. The semantic checks still need to occur before rendering. The long-term architecture therefore pairs structured syntax with checked lowering. 
 The Milestone 1 result 
 The broad local native baseline closed at ea4cc006f973632c4c7b1fb4569af2b4c93ff38a. Publication followed at a5ee30f171322f07c06e3846117f20c9e075ef95 on October 2. Historical notes record 128 generated sources and 410 workspace test/doc-test groups. 
 The milestone used private IR schema 6 and runtime ABI 3. Its wrapper forced skip-zk. That is an essential scope boundary when reading the early success report. 
 What was solved 
 Compact could generate useful typed Rust that executed a supported contract subset natively through the ledger runtime. The compiler boundary became inspectable, and new source cases had named owners. 
 What was still open 
 Recording a transcript, preparing a call, generating a proof and applying a funded transaction were later deliveries. Native execution established an important foundation for them.

title: Recording is an execution
text:
A correct result still leaves a missing statement 
 A native function can return the expected value without retaining the operations needed for proof preparation. Re-running the function elsewhere also risks observing a different state or a different witness result. 
 The project introduced recorded execution as an explicit result. Execute against a context, retain the ordered ledger trace, and return both the native result and its recording. Replay then checks that the operations reproduce the expected public transition. 
 Before and after · A counter advances from 1 to 2 
 Before · Observe the answer 
 A caller can see the return value and the new counter. To explain the public transition later, it needs the starting context and the exact operations the circuit performed. 
 After · Keep the operations from that execution 
  Illustrative recording
initial round = 1
  increment round by 1
expected final round = 2
  
   
  Mermaid source  
 Replay gives a second check on the public transition. A reader can see both what the call returned and how it moved the ledger. The proof and funded transaction add their own checks later. 
 Give the ledger slot an owner 
 Typed field descriptors connect a source declaration to its physical ledger path. A CellSlot knows the value type and where the VM should read or write. Generated code supplies arguments and propagates the returned context. 
 That division prevents arbitrary path arithmetic from spreading across generated bodies. It also creates a reusable boundary for witness ledger views and public state inspection. 
 Keep procedural macros mechanical 
 Derive macros add representation rules for generated types. They can implement a checked cell codec or enum representation. A body-wide macro that interprets contract semantics would hide another compiler inside generated Rust. 
 The selected design uses a typed runtime DSL and narrow derives. The compiler owns the source program and its admitted operations. The runtime owns execution and representation primitives. 
 From a recording to a deployed operation 
 An observed call must bind the installed contract state and operation. The expected verifier belongs to that operation. Proof preparation needs to preserve that relationship when it constructs a statement. 
 Wallet-facing work added deployment and subsequent-call handoff, state observations, typed reads, and the metadata needed to build later calls from confirmed state. That made the generated API useful beyond isolated examples. A historical ABI 28 Counter observation recorded round advancing from 1 to 2. Indexed actions were bound to the final merged transaction hash and checked through a trusted node/indexer. That observation did not provide authenticated consensus finality. 
 Milestone 2 closes a scoped target 
 By October 6 at 03c03a39a2d39c43c91143b9526ca1c2ffae706c, compactc --target rust emitted a crate, matching runtime material, proving artifacts and a manifest. The historical closeout records private IR 20, runtime ABI 49 and compiler 0.31.133. 
 The inventory covered 217 sources, 196 compiled roots and 755 exports. All 386 proof-required exports were available, alongside 369 non-proof exports. Sampled behavior covered 37 sources and 203 rows. Selected original proof/application cases and historical wallet observations supplied deeper evidence. Ten required remote workflows passed at the accepted head. 
 Availability, sampled behavior and selected proof coverage remain separate quantities. Keeping those columns prevented the closeout from turning a useful target into an unsupported whole-language claim.

title: Closing 0.3.0
text:
Why broaden the acceptance surface 
 A generated Counter is a useful vertical slice. Real users also need understandable generated APIs, compatibility checks, examples, diagnostics, package layout, application fixtures and proof consumers. 
 The 0.3.0 milestone brought those concerns into an explicit acceptance crosswalk. The team could then ask whether each promised outcome had code, tests, documentation and qualification evidence. 
 Real applications expose different pressure 
 DID and Passport exercised different application cohorts. DID covered twelve stateful exports with bounded native/recorded scenarios and proof receipts. The accepted Passport cohort covered 75 pure exports and had zero proof applicability. Together they exposed API and representation assumptions that a tiny circuit never touches. 
 Adoption was scoped. A proof-eligible selected export does not make every large contract cheap to prove. A partial contract exercise also needs to remain identified as such. Resource limits and the selected proof profile constrain what a local run establishes. 
 The importance of preserving a failed run 
 The closeout retained the original failed full run at revision 551f065c. Its final qualification joined the 423 successful unchanged-prefix commands with three recovery commands at the named source. 
 That is more informative than deleting failure evidence and showing a green badge. It explains which inputs and source remained valid, where repairs entered, and why the composite receipt was accepted. 
 Scope changes are engineering decisions 
 ACC was explicitly removed from the 0.3.0 accepted scope after the construct inventory found no unique witness, struct or ledger mechanism requiring another qualification family. Its exact application composition remained unqualified. Decoder resource containment also had an explicit boundary, with broader aggregate containment left for follow-up. 
 A milestone can close responsibly when its agreed outcomes are satisfied and its excluded work is documented. Reopening the same accepted work without a new defect would slow the next milestone while adding little confidence. 
 The October 9 closure 
 The milestone label was 0.3.0, while the Rust packages remained version 0.2.0. The qualified compiler boundary used private IR 20 and runtime ABI 50. Qualified implementation f9a496660a4a69f4dd7c7927111767ad5c0c12b2 and closure 0d7610b2792d60fee5d3713d4eb0ede3c98cc82a define this checkpoint. The report records 19 required outcomes accepted, 136 issues closed and a 93-criterion crosswalk. 
 The accepted delivery was a dedicated working line and matching evidence. A broader merge or distribution decision remained its own operation. 
 What was better 
 The result was a usable, reviewed compiler target with a richer application corpus and an explicit compatibility story. Just as valuable was the discipline of retaining limitations beside the passing outcomes.

title: Operations instead of shapes
text:
Before · Recognize the whole circuit 
 The early recorder worked like a set of templates. It inspected a circuit’s parameters, ledger actions and return value, then chose a recipe for a known pattern. The recipe could enforce the exact type and physical ledger slot. A different arrangement of familiar operations could still fail to find a recipe. 
   
  Mermaid source  
 Two shapes the old recorder knew 
 The Set insert comes from the historical oracle fixture. The Field example illustrates the saved-read pattern. Both excerpts omit their ledger declarations. 
 
 
 
 Shape 
 What the recognizer looked for 
 
 
 
 
 Insert into an opaque-string Set 
 One string parameter, exactly one insertion of that parameter into the declared Set slot, then a Unit result. A related membership shape expected no write and returned the membership Boolean. 
 
 
 Read an old Field value, update state and return the old value 
 A root binding that reads a declared Field cell once, actions inside that binding, then a return of the saved Field value. 
 
 
 
  // Shape 1 · The value inserted comes directly from the parameter.
export circuit addName(name: Opaque<"string">): [] {
  names.insert(disclose(name));
}

// Shape 2 · The result is the value from before the write.
export circuit replaceValue(next: Field): Field {
  const before = state.read();
  state.write(disclose(next));
  return before;
}
  
 Here, a  shape  was a recognizer’s predicate over the existing circuit representation. The relevant entities were the circuit, its declarations, and the recording recipe selected by the recognizer. There was no common Shape object with child shapes that the compiler could assemble into a larger program. 
 After · Build a plan from typed operations 
 The replacement describes a circuit as an ordered plan. A  block  is a list of bindings plus a result. Each  binding  pairs an operation with a typed value and an IR location. A read produces a value other operations can use. A write updates a declared slot. An  if  operation contains two blocks. The validator checks both branches, including their result types, while execution takes only the selected branch. 
   
  Mermaid source  
  Illustrative plans using the integrated operation model

addName(name: OpaqueString)
_      : Unit  = SetInsert(names, name)
return Unit

replaceValue(next: Field)

before : Field = CellRead(state)
_      : Unit  = CellWrite(state, next)
return before
  
 The integrated model gives Set insertion and membership their own typed operations, with the Set slot and element as inputs. In the Field example, the write and the return each refer to their own value, so returning the saved read stays explicit. A read, write or assertion now has the same place in the model inside a branch as it does at the top level. The validator can reject a value used before its definition or incompatible branch results at the operation that introduces the problem. In the integrated design, a shared semantic fold walks the admitted operations for native and recorded execution. 
 Walkthrough · What a witness sees depends on order 
 The prototype’s original orderedObservation circuit writes state, then takes one of three paths. The old recorder refused this circuit when recording was required. The pilot admitted the same source using the checked operation plan. 
  const before = state.read();
state.write(before + 1);
if (disclose(selector) == 0) {
  const observed = mark();
  assert(disclose(observed) == 77, "unexpected mark");
  round.increment(2);
  return disclose(state.read() + observed);
}
  
 This excerpt is the first branch. The other live witness branch increments the round and writes the new state before calling mark(). A witness is a host-supplied function. Which ledger state it observes depends on the writes already performed in the selected branch. 
   
  Mermaid source  
 
 
 
 Prototype case 
 What the witness saw 
 Result 
 
 
 
 
 Selector 0, next = 9 
 State 1 and round 0 
 Returns 78. State stays 1 and round ends at 2. 
 
 
 Selector 1, next = 9 
 State 12 and round 3 
 Returns 12. State stays 12 and round stays 3. 
 
 
 Selector 2 with next = 0 
 No witness call 
 Returns 3 and restores state to 0. 
 
 
 
 The cases start from the fixture’s zero state and round. The tests compared native and recorded execution with an independent TypeScript reference, including witness order, ledger state and gas. This pilot established execution and replay behavior. Its proof obligation remained separate. 
 Why a versioned IR matters here 
 Every new node has consequences for traversal, validation, lowering, capabilities and diagnostics. Exhaustive handling makes those obligations visible. A version change can state that the boundary has changed instead of letting a consumer guess from generated text. 
 Source spans matter for the same reason. An unsupported child expression should point back to Compact source. A Rust panic or a generic target failure leaves users debugging the implementation rather than their program. 
 Retire a recognizer with evidence 
 A recognizer can be removed after the new composition covers its accepted family. That requires inclusion checks across the old family's behavior, diagnostics and resource refusals. Deleting a special case after proving one happy example would lose useful support. 
 The retirement programme therefore worked through bounded operation families and explicit refusal controls. A capability book and shared registry made admission easier to inspect. 
 Local prototype to integrated change 
 The October 14 storybook froze f3cef799 while final effect qualification was still open. The later integrated commit 0437c894cd069af475bd8d5b254c24cc73615a09 on October 16 records the checked-effect replacement through PR #641. 
 This is a good example of why a living book needs dated chapters. The old snapshot accurately described a prototype. The continuation records its later integration. 
 What was solved 
 Operations became reusable components of larger contract behavior. Native and recorded execution could share semantic ownership, and retirement acquired a measurable obligation. 
 What remained 
 A compositional foundation still needs specific source features, result conversions, public interfaces and proof gates. The following iterations show that work in concrete terms.

title: The functional Ledger 8 line
text:
The next experiment 
 With checked effects available, the team explored an immutable Ledger 8 program request interpreted through shared execution logic. Native and recorded target adapters could consume the same admitted request while retaining their different output responsibilities. 
 This aimed to reduce the amount of contract-specific generated control flow. It also made the programme's operation inventory available for review. 
 An illustrative consumer shape is shown below. Constructing the immutable request performs no effects. Executing it against a context performs the admitted programme. 
  let request = replace::Program::new(next);
let recorded = request.execute_recorded(context)?;
  
 The generated module and parameter types depend on the contract. The example shows the ownership boundary and is not a standalone runnable contract. 
 Keep metadata out of the execution body 
 Review metadata is useful for auditing a generated programme. Large strings and inventories can also dominate an otherwise small Rust file. 
 The follow-up separated metadata assets while retaining stable public access, exact identities and execution behavior. That made generated code easier to read without erasing the material needed for review. 
 Witnesses and effects still need order 
 An immutable description does not make execution order irrelevant. Witness callbacks can return values and update private state. Ledger operations observe and change public state. A Unit-valued call may still have an essential effect. 
 Later slices preserved ordered Unit initializers, terminal effects, tuple returns and named bind receivers. Each one corrected a boundary where a superficially small expression could lose behavior during lowering. 
 From the prototype to the working branch 
 The October 18 local prototype checkpoint was documented at ec7262e49 with an explicit experimental flag and Ledger 8.1.3 scope. The historical note records 3,299 workspace passes, seven manual ignores, and generated scenarios across four routes. 
 The working branch integration c353907d8c323db16eedb35d5a7f0151aab859bb records that transition on October 27. Earlier typed effects, witnesses and collection work from October 18–19 was included in the reviewed baseline. Subsequent PRs added Fold, Map size, projections, DID and SDK consumers. 
 What was better 
 The programme model made native and recording behavior easier to relate. The generated API could express a request whose operations had already passed semantic checks, with review material outside its main execution text. 
 What remained 
 The broader functional scope was a proposal with its own acceptance work. A narrow prototype result could not silently establish the entire roadmap. Source admission and proof coverage continued as independent deliveries.

title: Ergonomics, one semantic gap at a time
text:
Make ordinary usage behave ordinarily 
 A type-safe backend becomes ergonomic when familiar source expressions compile to predictable APIs. Constant-valued Vector projections, nested Map size expressions and direct Fold are examples. They are small at the source level and cross several implementation owners. 
 The work kept each gap bounded. Determine the Compact semantics, extend the checked representation if necessary, lower into structured Rust, exercise the generated consumer, and run applicable proof and refusal controls. 
 Projection is not tuple selection 
 A source index into a fixed vector carries different type and result obligations from a tuple projection. Confusing them can make a generated value have the wrong shape even when one constant example works. 
 The accepted projection slice retained that distinction. Nested Map size and Fold then reused the checked foundation while adding their own ownership and effect requirements. 
 Before and after · Index a Vector by a named constant 
 Before · Use the position directly 
 A literal made the fixed position visible to the Rust backend. A source program using a constant expression could hit an unsupported projection even though the position was knowable during compilation. 
  // Illustrative literal-index version.
export pure circuit first(items: Vector<2, Field>): Field {
  return items[0];
}
  
 After · Let the compiler work out the position 
  // From the accepted fixture. Idx is an alias for Uint<8>.
export pure circuit first(items: Vector<2, Field>): Field {
  const i: Idx = 1;
  const index = i * 0;
  return items[index];
}
  
 For input [7, 9], both versions select 7. The second version lets the programmer name and calculate the position. The same slice checks bounds and keeps dynamic indices outside this fixed-position feature. 
 Wide multiplication by zero 
 A wide unsigned result cannot always be squeezed into a convenient native integer. Multiplying by zero still has a precise result type and output geometry. 
 PR #700 preserved that typed zero behavior. The review also retained a known limit around stateful zero-width results and frontend/ZKIR commitment agreement. The selected proof APIs declare Uint<8> results and establish those statements. They do not settle general zero-width proof readiness. 
 Product and Vector widening 
 Many later slices concern a value that is valid in a wider expected context. The tricky cases involve nested products, aliases, literals and constructor loops. A widening has to preserve both value semantics and effects. 
 PR #703 reconciled an outer-Vector stack with the canonical backend. PR #704 added Linux proof coverage for eligible cases. PR #705 and its follow-ups qualified constructor Vector expressions and typed equality guards. 
 CI belongs to the slice 
 A logical slice includes its tests, documentation, review and integration result. Long and fragile CI motivated local work and measured job ownership. PR #716 split qualification into measured owners, while PR #723 reused an exact Nix compiler environment across consumers. 
 The goal was to reduce repeated preparation while retaining complete required gates. It was not permission to replace semantic tests with a faster badge. 
 What was better 
 More ordinary Compact programs reached typed generated Rust without ad hoc source rewrites. Each slice retained source/API/refusal qualification and proof/application evidence for selected applicable statements.

title: Ledger 9 is a protocol migration
text:
Why a branch boundary mattered 
 Ledger 9 adoption began on a dedicated line so the Ledger 8 implementation and its evidence remained available. Changing a dependency family can affect state tags, serialization, gas, proof version, fee material, transaction APIs and installed operations. 
 Rust source compilation alone would establish only a small part of that migration. 
 The dependency and ABI contract 
 The runtime adopted the published Ledger 9.1.0.1 package set. The compiler/runtime pairing moved to ABI 54, ordinary Rust generation selected ZKIR v3, and the workspace and Nix Rust tools moved to Rust 1.99.0. 
 The synchronous local Compact runtime used minor 0.17.0 with Onchain Runtime 4.0.1. Released Compact 0.36.0 used its own asynchronous runtime pairing. Comparing them required matching captures and explicit adapters, with cross-version refusal controls. 
 A failing transaction exposed an emitter bug 
 The initial standalone Counter proof passed, but transaction proving exhausted its skip entries. The earlier emitter grouped expanded ledger operations into one impact. Ledger 9 consumes a skip entry for each transcript operation. 
 The repair preserved those boundaries and omitted suppressed operations. The Counter's three impacts then matched the released reference. This is a particularly useful migration lesson. A proof result from an isolated statement can pass while the transaction consumer exposes an incompatibility in the same generated circuit. 
 Before and after · Count the steps the prover reads 
 Before · Count one source action 
 Imagine one action expanding into three transcript operations, A, B and C. Grouping them together emitted one impact and provided one skip entry. The transaction prover consumed that entry for A and still needed entries for B and C. 
 After · Count each emitted operation 
 Emit one impact per active operation and omit suppressed operations. The repaired Counter had three impacts and matched the released reference. The lettering below explains the mapping without abbreviating the actual Counter transcript into invented instructions. 
   
  Mermaid source  
 Funding is part of the test 
 The Ledger 9 lane used released dust/10/spend material. The retained Ledger 8 dust/9/spend material belonged to the historical line. The contract verifier and the Dust verifier also serve different roles. 
 The qualified Counter run generated fresh keys and a standalone proof. A separate process verified that proof and refused changed bindings, commitment, wrong verifier and corrupt bytes. A separately proved, Dust-funded transaction then passed default strictness, applied the expected state and refused exact replay with unchanged ledger bytes. 
 The integrated local result 
 At frozen source 9409b7da1cc652940469903a8380000b0b707239, the full local parity gate on macOS arm64 with Rust 1.99.0 checked 286 fixtures and bound 87 generated consumers to their executed artifacts. Checked recording was observed for 688 selected exports, including 626 proof-eligible exports. 
 Nine child proof gates passed for 87 selected calls. Those counts overlap across gates and belong to that frozen revision. They are not an aggregate count of every later compatibility proof. 
 Foundation publication 
 PR #725 merged on November 12. The publication and CI repair history belongs to that PR. The extensive subsequent upstream ports remained a separate local compatibility milestone. 
 The book therefore marks the foundation as merged and the later corpus work as local qualification. It makes no new claim about every final-head CI result from a historical local receipt. 
  Compare the same Counter call in Ledger 8 TypeScript and Ledger 9 Rust .

title: One Counter, two backends
Porting the cryptographic surface
text:
A curve name is only the beginning 
 Supporting P-256 or secp256k1 means more than exposing a verification function. The compiler needs source types, defaults, casts and operations. Generated Rust needs distinct carriers. The runtime needs checked decoders and ledger layouts. ZKIR must receive the intended operands. Witnesses and public interfaces must preserve their representation. 
 The migration proceeded through those layers in small families. 
 Fields before points 
 Base and scalar fields have different moduli. Rust types preserve that distinction, so an ordinary call cannot accidentally substitute one carrier for another. Explicit source casts have their defined modular behavior. An untrusted host decoder still needs a canonicality check. 
 Foreign field ledger transport also uses shifted values and split atoms. For the selected K1 and P-256 layouts, the low and high parts occupy 24 and 8 bytes. A plain integer comparison would miss a representation error. 
 Before and after · Make the curve part of the type 
 Before · A byte string needs context 
 Consider a host program with bytes from two curves. Both values can be held in a byte array. The caller has to remember which one belongs with the next operation. 
 After · A generated call can express the distinction 
  // Schematic Rust. Names illustrate the roles in the API.
fn multiply_k1(point: K1Point, scalar: K1Scalar) -> K1Point;

multiply_k1(k1_point, k1_scalar);   // The carriers match.
multiply_k1(k1_point, p256_scalar); // Type error.
  
 The example uses schematic names because the exact API depends on the generated interface. The ordinary typed call rejects the mix-up during compilation. Data arriving from outside Rust still needs the runtime’s canonical decoding and point validation. 
 Unary and guarded operations 
 Inversion of zero must fail on an active path, including when the result is discarded. A proof VM may evaluate an operation eagerly even when source control flow makes its result inactive. 
 Guarded lowering therefore supplies a typed neutral input to the inactive operation while preserving active-path refusal. These cases show why the source semantics, host runtime and constraint model need to be checked together. 
 Points and group operations 
 The K1 and P-256 families added typed point construction, equality, coordinate access, addition, multiplication and generator multiplication. Tests cover identity, off-curve input, coordinate-specific refusal and cross-curve rejection. 
 Curve25519 adds subgroup and encoding obligations. Its scalar transport splits at bit 204, and its point transport uses four shifted Base atoms. The original generator and its double passed ordinary Rust, recording and VM replay. 
 Signatures, hashes and recovery 
 K1 ECDSA and Ethereum address derivation retain the original message and byte-order rules. P-256 ECDSA uses the upstream Compact implementation, with known-answer and Wycheproof accounting. Ed25519 uses SHA-512 and canonical scalar conversion, with identity and mixed-order key refusals. 
 The host recovery helper returns a checked point. In the K1 owner-binding fixture, the recovery ID guides a witness, and the circuit authenticates that point through its signature and derived address. P-256 host recovery remains a host API with its own tests. Applications requiring a specific signer must compare the recovered key to their trusted key. 
 Honest corpus accounting 
 The P-256 report accounts for 484 Wycheproof vectors. It drives 265 through the selected circuit interface and records 219 encoding exclusions. The driven outcomes include true, false, scalar-boundary refusal and abort. 
 An excluded encoding is part of the coverage report. It should not be counted as a successful in-circuit test. The same discipline applies to intact fixtures whose newer language pragma remains refused. 
 Selected proof depth 
 Local arm64 lanes include independent proofs and funded transactions for selected field, point, group, signature and recovery statements. The sequential signature fixtures also preserve witness order and substituted-key refusals. 
 The complete original group and mixed-circuit proof matrix remains open. The available typed APIs and selected proof evidence are substantial, with scope determined by each receipt.

title: Wire values, events and state
text:
Serialization is an API 
 An encoding determines what a verifier and another implementation will receive. Boolean encoding must admit its defined values. Enum encoding must use the declaration's ordinal bounds. Products must preserve element order and padding. Wide integers must retain their full width. 
 The migration implemented Boolean, fixed Bytes, native Uint and Field, product encoders/decoders, enum ordinals, wide Uint through 248 bits, foreign base/scalar fields and empty vectors. 
 Empty does not mean invalid 
 A zero-length vector occupies no wire bytes even when its element type lacks a codec. That is a real source-language edge case, and both mainstream references compile the empty point-vector fixture. 
 The tested JubjubScalar wire probes instead fail internally in the pinned mainstream source and released binary. The local branch gives a source error. This is recorded as a known boundary rather than inventing codec compatibility. 
 A leading character can be protocol data 
 The opaque-string regression concerns a leading U+FEFF. A decoder that strips it can change a receipt, archived value, equality result or Map key. 
 The intact fixture exercises those operations in sequence. Six proof preimages, independent proofs and separately funded applications preserve the original value. A consistently stripped value may form a different valid statement. The test must bind the honest proof to the original statement to detect that substitution. 
 Byte equality is content equality 
 Two separately allocated Uint8Arrays with identical bytes should compare according to Compact's value semantics. The TypeScript path previously exposed a reference-equality mismatch. 
 The port checks length and contents, including values nested in products and vectors. All 23 original cases passed generated execution, SDK preflight, independent proofs and funded strict replay checks. The unchanged Rust and raw ZKIR outputs made the location of the fix particularly clear. 
 Before and after · Compare bytes from two sources 
 Before · Two objects with the same contents compare unequal 
  // This JavaScript example reproduces the reference-equality pitfall.
const stored = new Uint8Array([4, 8]);
const received = new Uint8Array([4, 8]);
stored === received; // false
  
 After · Compare the byte sequence 
  // The behavior the generated comparison must preserve.
stored.length === received.length &&
  stored.every((byte, index) => byte === received[index]); // true
  
 Changing the second byte to 9 produces false. The same rule applies when the arrays appear inside a product or Vector. The Compact source compares the values directly, and generated code supplies the value semantics. 
 Events are ordered effects 
 The event migration covered ShieldedSpend, ShieldedBurn, ShieldedMint, ShieldedReceive, their unshielded counterparts, Paused, Unpaused and Misc. Each event has its own tag and payload. 
 Optional and Either fields preserve inactive bytes as required by the source representation. Disclosure analysis must also inspect those fields. A branch that is inactive at runtime cannot become a way to hide undeclared witness disclosure. 
 SDK controls substitute a tag, byte field, domain separator, recipient or event order. The selected funded transaction tests inspect the emitted ledger events and replay behavior. 
 Nested defaults are observable 
 A historic Merkle tree default inside a Map begins with empty history. A top-level reset has its own blank-root behavior. Reusing the wrong constructor can produce a plausible tree with the wrong historic semantics. 
 Both intact plain and historic upstream fixtures now generate typed Rust nested slots. Their eight original exports have selected fresh proof and funded application coverage on arm64. 
 Later qualification receipts 
 The later BOM receipt at 360af593b records six proofs and six funded export calls. The nested Merkle receipt at 3a178e916 records eight proofs and eight funded calls. Opaque-byte equality at 7a4fab772 records 23 of each. These source-specific results supersede the earlier open-proof descriptions preserved in the plan snapshot. 
 The  public delivery register  retains the receipt identities and selected funded-result summaries without witness or key material.

title: Cross-contract calls and the held boundary
text:
The attractive surface 
 A generated method that calls another contract looks like a small API feature. Its semantics include the callee address, declared interface, installed operation, expected verifier, entrypoint identity, arguments, result and communication commitment. 
 A call that accidentally reaches a same-shaped sibling entrypoint could produce the same host result while proving a different assertion. 
 Start from the mainstream implementation 
 The owner directed the team to read and port mainstream's sequence carefully. Resolve the module and interface. Authenticate the operation and expected verifier. Enter the callee's context. Restore the caller. Propagate the result and commitment opening through the caller's witness. 
 This avoids inventing an independent interpretation of a cross-contract call. 
 What is already available 
 Typed address comparisons, entrypoint hash binding, native claim recording and replay are implemented prerequisites. The runtime can prepare a supplied caller and leaf-callee recording from a shared ledger snapshot. 
 Preparation checks the installed verifiers and the exact claim before using Ledger 9's joint partitioner. The pair-preparation tests use synthetic verifier carriers and cover honest preparation and refusal controls. 
 The internal compiler statement probe also produced a selected standalone caller proof with an adapter-built preimage. Same-output sibling entrypoint, wrong verifier, binding and corruption controls passed for that bounded statement. 
 Before and after · Two entrypoints return the same value 
 Before · Comparing the answer leaves an identity gap 
 Suppose a caller expects entrypoint A, and sibling B accepts the same arguments and also returns 7. A test that checks only the 7 would pass even if the wrong entrypoint supplied it. 
 After · Preparation checks which entrypoint produced the claim 
   
  Mermaid source  
 The pair-preparation tests exercise the check on supplied recordings. The selected standalone statement also refuses the same-output sibling. The next section records where that check still needs to reach ordinary generated calls. 
 What is still held 
 Ordinary generated invocation of the intact caller and a real joint funded two-contract transaction remain on hold. The canonical worktree preserves three uncommitted compiler files for this direction. 
 Runtime preparation of supplied recordings is a useful prerequisite. It does not establish that the generated source call constructs those recordings correctly. 
 The eventual acceptance path 
 Resume with the original caller/callee fixtures, the sibling substitution test and the pinned reference implementation. Qualify generated execution in both targets. Prove both statements, independently verify them, apply the funded joint transaction, then check replay, rollback and invalid bindings. 
 The intact transfer model measures k=9 and belongs in an explicit slow lane. 
 Why this boundary improves the API 
 An ergonomic contract method becomes trustworthy when its ordinary call path carries the same authentication and statement identity that the low-level runtime requires. Explicit types can prevent ordinary family mix-ups. Installed state and untrusted artifacts still require runtime validation.

title: A proof is one stage
text:
Follow one circuit all the way 
 The pipeline explorer shows eight stages. Each stage has an owner, a useful output and a failure that the next stage can expose. 
 Source admission 
 The frontend checks Compact syntax, types, disclosure and supported target capabilities. A newer language pragma may fail before a circuit is considered. A derivative with that pragma removed is useful for investigating semantics, with its changed source identity recorded explicitly. 
 Typed lowering and Rust emission 
 The internal IR preserves types and operations, and carries source origins where the frontend supplies them. Checked lowering establishes a Rust representation and legal control flow. Syntax emission renders the admitted model. Generated code compilation catches Rust-level errors in the public API. Structural and type checks do not establish source semantic equivalence. A same-typed operand or slot substitution needs an independent behavioral observation. 
 Native execution 
 Execute the generated function against the selected ledger runtime. Compare returns, state, witnesses, private state and gas with an independent reference case. 
 Recorded execution and replay 
 Record the same admitted effects and replay them through the ledger VM. Compare the resulting state and ordered observations. Losing a Unit-valued effect can be detected here even when the return value looks harmless. 
 SDK preflight 
 Interpret the exact ZKIR against the serialized preimage. Check its raw identities and compare input, output, public transcript and private transcript fields. Mutated statements should be refused when they violate the original circuit. 
 Fresh standalone proof and verification 
 Generate the selected keys from pinned parameters and exact IR. Produce a new proof. Verify in an independent process with the verifier rederived from those identities. Exercise wrong-verifier, changed-binding and corrupt-proof controls. 
 Funded transaction 
 Construct a separate transaction-bound proof. Preserve the observed installed operation. Include genuine fee funding and default-strict ledger verification. Compare the applied state and events to generated native execution. 
 Replay and rollback 
 Apply the same verified transaction again. The accepted result in the selected lanes is IntentAlreadyExists with unchanged whole-ledger bytes and no repeated events. A broader transaction failure may also require rollback tests. 
 Before and after · What does “the proof passed” tell you? 
 Before · Verify one statement in isolation 
 For Counter, a valid standalone proof established its selected statement. The transaction prover still exposed the missing skip entries described in the Ledger 9 chapter. 
 After · Test the two paths separately 
   
  Mermaid source  
 
 
 
 Test 
 What the reader can look for 
 
 
 
 
 Verify the standalone proof 
 The verifier, bindings and proof bytes match the intended statement. 
 
 
 Prove and apply a funded transaction 
 The ledger accepts the transaction under default strictness and reaches the expected state. 
 
 
 Submit the same transaction again 
 The ledger refuses the replay and leaves the state unchanged. 
 
 
 
 Why compile-fail tests belong in the guide 
 The generated Rust API should reject invalid ordinary use at compile time where the type system can express the constraint. Passing a P-256 carrier to a K1 method is one example. 
 Unknown bytes, installed verifier material and decoded protocol data cross untrusted boundaries. Those inputs need explicit diagnostics and runtime errors. A useful API makes that distinction predictable. 
 A review checklist 
 
 Identify the exact source, compiler, backend, runtime and SDK family. 
 Check the affected ordinary entry points, including previously generated consumers. 
 Inspect positive behavior and the most relevant invalid-use controls. 
 Bind raw IR, generated library, keys, parameters and immutable verifier identity. 
 Read the actual application and replay receipts. 
 State the platform and the source revision for every aggregate count.

title: The next reader inherits a map
text:
The state at this edition 
 The Ledger 9 migration foundation is merged through PR #725. The later compatibility programme has local arm64 evidence for large portions of cryptography, hashing, serialization, collections, event semantics and generated Rust/TypeScript parity. 
 The frozen local compatibility cutoff for this edition is 7a4fab772ee34c19053ce293d08052b501ce4b50. The signed isolated Jubjub identity-key assertion and Keccak opaque diagnostic commits are recorded separately at 6eef58425bb53883c8f3b417b601246820c7d675 and 30a2d76550beb7d920a92bab2be6b1180243f658. 
 Their local review follow-ups were resolved in checkpoint v73. They await canonical integration and final qualification. 
 The remaining milestone 
 The programme still needs complete applicable upstream corpus accounting, the semantics required for intact newer-language admission, remaining fixture-specific proof matrices, required native Linux qualification, and the held generated two-contract path. 
 The local frontend's language gate remains 0.23.105 while the pinned main reference uses 0.28.0. Editing a version number would not establish the intervening semantics. The history inventory identifies the changes that must be ported and tested. 
 How commits become iterations 
 Use the commit explorer to find the implementation and its follow-up repairs. A logical iteration usually includes a semantic gap, affected owners, positive and refusal tests, documentation, independent review and applicable proof/integration results. 
 Several commits can therefore belong to one iteration. A milestone includes several accepted iterations and an explicit scope. Git merge commits identify integration points, while author dates describe the original work. The explorer labels its date field accordingly. 
 Keep local history durable 
 The book includes a frozen commit catalogue and public narrative snapshots for local work. Published commits link to GitHub. Commits known only from local refs retain their identities and metadata in the catalogue, with publication status shown explicitly. 
 The source snapshots carry selected plan and qualification summaries. They provide a durable public account without embedding machine paths, private witness values, keys or complete internal notes. 
 The maintainers' continuation rule 
 Update the edition manifest when taking a new snapshot. Preserve accepted historical reports. Add a correction when new evidence changes an earlier interpretation. Keep the book's status vocabulary aligned with the actual evidence. 
 A claim that was locally valid in October may remain useful in November. Its source, platform and scope let a future engineer decide whether it applies to the next change. 
 Why this journey is worth preserving 
 The strongest thread is the steady movement of hidden assumptions into explicit owners. Source semantics moved into checked IR. Rust syntax moved into syntax trees. Ledger operations moved into typed slots and effect programmes. Proof and application identities moved into retained receipts. 
 That makes future work easier to reason about. The next engineer receives a map of decisions, tests and boundaries, with the unfinished work still visible.

title: The October architecture
text:
Historical atlas. This chapter preserves the October 14 documentation cutoff. The main narrative records subsequent deliveries and current limits. 
 Source snapshot —  original chapter at 51a079bd . The documented implementation cutoff is f3cef799 on October 14. The documentation snapshot and implementation revision are distinct. 
 
 The current conceptual pipeline 
  Compact source
    │
    ▼
Chez Scheme parser, type checker and shared analysis
    │  Lnodisclose + source-owner metadata
    ▼
private versioned Rust IR (JSON)
    │  strict serde model + resource preflight
    ├──────────────────────────────┐
    ▼                              ▼
native semantic fold         recording effect lowering
    │                              │
    │                        checked RecordedPlan
    └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                   ▼
          syn / quote Rust AST
                   │
             prettyplease
                   ▼
      generated Rust crate + manifest
                   │
      midnight-compact-runtime
                   │
 official ledger-8 VM / state / FAB / crypto / ZK
  
 “IR schema 20” in the closed Rust-AST milestones means the twentieth revision
of this private Chez-to-Rust interchange. It is not Compact language version
20 and not a universally recognized specification level. 
 Why syntax trees mattered 
  syn  does not prove that generated code is semantically correct. What it does
is move an important class of failure earlier: output is constructed as Rust
syntax rather than assembled as strings.  quote  and  proc-macro2  make larger
fragments composable;  prettyplease  makes the resulting syntax readable and
deterministic. 
 The stronger guarantee comes from the surrounding discipline: 
 
 the IR enums are closed and reject unknown fields; 
 types, actions and expressions have explicit variants; 
 resource preflight bounds depth, nodes and call expansion; 
 malformed IR is an error, while unsupported recording is a typed capability
  outcome; 
 generated fixtures compile and execute; snapshots alone are not acceptance. 
 
 Four execution layers that must not be conflated 
 
 
 
 Layer 
 Question 
 Owner 
 
 
 
 
 Native execution 
 Can the typed Compact operation run and return the right state/value? 
 Generated code + native runtime 
 
 
 Recording 
 Can execution produce a complete ordered public VM/FAB trace? 
 Checked recording plan + runtime frame 
 
 
 Preparation and replay 
 Does that trace replay against observed state and the selected verifier? 
 Runtime transaction adapter 
 
 
 Proof/application 
 Can the exact artifacts prove, verify and apply under the pinned ledger policy? 
 Prover, verifier and ledger 
 
 
 
 A native method can exist without recording. A recorded method can exist when
proof material is absent. A successful proof preparation is not a submitted or
finalized network transaction. The documentation and capability reports keep
these distinctions because collapsing them created misleading coverage claims
early in the project. 
 Before: shape recognition 
  Stateful circuit
  ├─ is this a voting shape?
  ├─ is this a guarded optional write?
  ├─ is this a shielded payout?
  ├─ is this funded mint?
  └─ otherwise: legacy fallback or structured refusal
  
 This model is safe when every admitted shape is tightly tested, but its reuse
unit is too large. Supporting  MapLookup , a witness and an assertion in three
separate profiles does not prove that a fourth arrangement composes correctly. 
 After: checked effects 
  Stateful circuit
  │
  ├─ resolve declarations and lexical identities
  ├─ type each value and operation
  ├─ compose ordered effects and returns
  ├─ validate resource, scope and replay invariants
  └─ render only the complete checked plan
  
 The effect vocabulary is intentionally not a new ledger. It references runtime
operations whose semantics remain owned by the pinned Midnight primitives.
The plan owns compiler facts: types, source order, bindings, effects, result
roles, admissibility and the precise reason a supported native operation is not
recordable. 
 Source provenance: current truth 
 Published Rust-AST work carries source-owner file, line and column information
through the private IR and uses structural paths in typed recording gaps. At
the prototype cutoff, the accepted closure plan still describes these as
declaration locations—not arbitrary nested expression ranges. 
 Original occurrence tracking and authenticated source views prevent tests from
quietly replacing genuine frontend artifacts with convenient hand-built JSON.
The separate transient-value origin proposal remains a proposal unless a later
qualified candidate demonstrates it. Publication must never expose absolute
checkout paths, secrets, witness values or private proof material. 
 Generated API and runtime ownership 
 Generated crates expose typed Compact values, witnesses, native entry points,
recorded calls where available, and transaction preparation helpers under the
matching runtime ABI. The runtime owns reusable representation and integration
mechanics: bounded integers, fixed bytes/vectors, ledger ADT access, FAB
alignment, VM programs, recording frames, verifier decoding and optional
transaction construction. 
 That ownership is a trade-off. Generated code becomes smaller and more regular;
the runtime becomes a safety-critical compatibility layer. This is why runtime
ABI, dependency graph and exact ledger/proof versions are tested independently
from the compiler IR schema.
